title: Provable Classical and Quantum Local Algorithms for Max-$k$-Cut and Quantum Advantage at Moderate Girth
authors: Anuj Apte, Abid Khan, Edward Farhi, Kunal Marwaha, Sami Boulebnane, Ruslan Shaydulin
abstract: Broadening the study of quantum optimization algorithms from binary to $k$-element alphabets has been shown to open new avenues for potential quantum advantage. A quantum advantage claim for approximate optimization requires showing that, under the same assumptions, an efficient quantum algorithm provably achieves a better performance than can be proven for the best known efficient classical algorithms. We study local classical and quantum algorithms for Max-$k$-Cut on $d$-regular graphs of girth $g$. We advance classical algorithms for this problem by developing a local vector algorithm based on the explicit vector construction of Thompson, Parekh, and Marwaha (TPM). Our algorithm gives the best provable cut fraction guarantee among known efficient classical algorithms on regular graphs for $k\geq3$. To evaluate the performance of QAOA under identical assumptions of girth and regularity, we develop tensor network techniques for general $d$ and $k \geq 2$. In addition, using an equivalence to a coupled qudit--boson system, we compute the QAOA performance in the infinite-degree limit. Together, these techniques give provable guarantees on QAOA performance on large graphs. Despite the improvements we introduce to the classical algorithm, QAOA achieves a better cut fraction guarantee for depths $p\geq 9$, corresponding to girth $g\geq 20$, for both finite- and infinite-degree regimes. Thus, we obtain an apparent quantum advantage from applying QAOA to the Max-$k$-Cut problem.
summary: This paper rigorously compares the performance of classical and quantum algorithms for the Max-$k$-Cut problem on structured graphs. By developing an improved local vector algorithm and analyzing QAOA using tensor networks, the authors provide provable guarantees. They conclude that QAOA surpasses the best classical bounds for sufficiently deep circuits, suggesting a concrete instance of quantum advantage.
main_problem: The paper develops and compares provable classical and quantum local algorithms for solving the Max-$k$-Cut problem on regular graphs.
main_result: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) achieves a better cut-fraction guarantee than the best known classical algorithm for sufficiently deep circuits ($p \ge 9$) on graphs with high girth, suggesting an apparent quantum advantage.
method: The authors employ a local vector algorithm generalizing TPM for the classical side, and they analyze QAOA performance using tensor network techniques and an equivalence to a coupled qudit–boson system for the quantum side.

key_observables: Cut fraction (ratio of cut edges to total edges) and the approximation ratio relative to the optimum $	ext{OPT}_k(G)$.
important_parameters: Number of subsets ($k$), graph degree ($d$), girth ($g$), and QAOA depth ($p$).
main_assumptions: The analysis simplifies by restricting to regular graphs with girth $g \ge 2p + 2$ to enable tree-like structure analysis for expectation values.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates Max-3-Cut on a small graph, and the paper references multiple tables (2-5) detailing cut fractions for Max-2, 3, and 4-Cut across varying depths and degrees.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the Max-$k$-Cut problem and compares it to SDP relaxations. It then details the development of an improved local vector algorithm for the classical bound. Finally, it analyzes QAOA performance using advanced techniques, culminating in a comparison showing quantum advantage for large girth.
why_interesting: The work directly compares the scaling and performance of quantum algorithms (QAOA) against state-of-the-art classical methods (local vector algorithms) for a fundamental NP-hard optimization problem, which is central to quantum computation theory.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Example of Max-3-Cut on a graph with 7 vertices and 11 edges. Vertices are assigned to subsets with labels {0, 1, 2}. Dashed edges connect vertices belonging to different sets (cut), while solid edges connect vertices of the same set (uncut).

Figure 2: Edge-centered tree structure for a 3-regular graph (d = 3) at depth p = 3. The edge {u, v} is at the center. Each endpoint branches into d −1 = 2 neighbors (excluding the central edge), and this branching continues for p levels. On a graph of girth ≥2p + 2 = 8, this neighborhood contains no cycles, enabling exact computation of edge expectations via tree tensor network contraction. The same structure governs both QAOA (where correlations are confined to this tree) and the vector algorithm (where vector coefficients depend only on distance from each vertex).

Figure 3: Vector assignment on the Petersen graph, a 3-regular graph with girth 5. Each vertex i gets a vector vi ∈R10 with entry α0 on coordinate i (self), entry α1 on coordinates corresponding to neighbors, and 0 elsewhere. Vertex 0 (blue) has neighbors {1, 4, 5}; vertex 1 (red) has neighbors {0, 2, 6}. These vertices share edge {0, 1} but no common neighbors (since girth ≥4), so v0 · v1 = 2α0α1.
